checks.prompt: Members of your ensemble have pairwise error correlation ρ = 0.9. You increase the ensemble from 4 members to 32. What happens to the error variance?
options: It barely moves — correlation sets a floor of ρ that no ensemble size can break through, so 32 members buy roughly a 10% reduction
It falls by a factor of 8, in proportion to the increase in members
It falls to 1/32 of a single model's variance, as the classic result predicts
It increases, because correlated members reinforce each other's errors
checks.explanation: Var(ensemble) = σ²·[ρ + (1−ρ)/N]. As N grows this tends to ρσ², not to zero. At ρ = 0.9 an infinite ensemble buys 10%. This is why ensembling five checkpoints from one training run usually 'barely helps' — they are highly correlated by construction.

checks.prompt: Explain the 'panel of specialists' analogy and how the same-basin versus different-basin distinction determines which ensembling technique is available to you.
checks.expected: A correct answer must convey that a panel is only worth more than one expert if the members were trained differently and therefore make DIFFERENT mistakes — five graduates of the same programme confidently make the same error, so you paid five fees for one opinion (this is what error correlation ρ measures). It must then link this to loss basins: independently-trained models land in DIFFERENT basins, so their weights cannot be averaged (the midpoint is the ridge between basins and the network is broken) and you must ensemble their OUTPUTS at N× inference cost. Fine-tunes from a shared checkpoint stay in the SAME basin, so their weights can be averaged directly — a model soup — giving a single model at 1× inference cost.
checks.explanation: Same basin or not is the single fact that tells you whether weight averaging is on the table.

checks.prompt: Three members predict class 0, class 0 and class 1, with the dissenter far more confident than the other two. How do probability-averaging and logit-averaging differ here?
options: Probability averaging acts like a vote and picks class 0; logit averaging is closer to a geometric mean and the confident dissenter can flip the result to class 1
They always agree on the argmax; they differ only in the confidence assigned to it
Logit averaging acts like a vote; probability averaging lets the most confident member dominate
Probability averaging is undefined when members disagree, which is why logit averaging is standard
checks.explanation: Averaging probabilities is an arithmetic mean, averaging logits is (up to normalisation) a geometric mean. They disagree exactly when the members disagree — the case you built the ensemble for. Neither is 'correct': probability averaging is more robust to an overconfident member, logit averaging propagates confidence and suits well-calibrated members.

checks.prompt: Write `ensemble_variance_ratio(rho, n)` returning the ensemble's error variance as a fraction of a single member's, for n members with pairwise error correlation rho: ρ + (1−ρ)/n. Standard library only.
checks.solution:
def ensemble_variance_ratio(rho, n):
    return rho + (1.0 - rho) / n
checks.test:
assert abs(ensemble_variance_ratio(0.0, 4) - 0.25) < 1e-12
assert abs(ensemble_variance_ratio(0.0, 32) - 1.0 / 32) < 1e-12
assert abs(ensemble_variance_ratio(0.5, 1) - 1.0) < 1e-12, 'N=1 is a no-op'
assert abs(ensemble_variance_ratio(0.9, 1) - 1.0) < 1e-12
assert abs(ensemble_variance_ratio(0.9, 10**9) - 0.9) < 1e-6, 'floor is rho'
assert ensemble_variance_ratio(0.3, 8) < ensemble_variance_ratio(0.3, 2)
for n in (2, 4, 8):
    assert ensemble_variance_ratio(0.9, n) > ensemble_variance_ratio(0.1, n)
checks.explanation: The N=1 cases are the sanity check: with one member the ratio must be exactly 1.0 for any ρ. The 10**9 case shows the floor — the limit is ρ, not zero, and that is the whole practical lesson.

checks.prompt: You average the weights of two models fine-tuned from DIFFERENT pretrained checkpoints. What should you expect?
options: A broken model — the midpoint between two loss basins is the ridge between them, and performance is far worse than either member
A model roughly as good as the average of the two members' performance
A model slightly better than either member, which is the usual model-soup result
An error at load time, because the weight tensors will have incompatible shapes
checks.explanation: Model soups require linear mode connectivity, which holds for fine-tunes of a SHARED checkpoint and not across independent pretraining runs. The notebook measures a soup loss of 3.66 against member losses of 0.02 and 0.15. Averaging their outputs instead would have been perfectly fine.

checks.prompt: Your actual goal is a model that is cheaper to serve. Ensembling makes inference more expensive. Explain the two ways ensembling still earns a place in a compression pipeline.
checks.expected: A correct answer must identify (1) ENSEMBLE-THEN-DISTIL: an ensemble is the cheapest way to build a teacher better than any single model you can train, and distillation then converts it into one student at 1× inference cost — this is how most of the value gets realised in production; and (2) MODEL SOUPS: averaging the weights of same-basin fine-tunes (for example the good runs of a hyperparameter sweep from one checkpoint) yields a single model at unchanged inference cost, for essentially one line of code plus a forward pass to recompute normalisation statistics. It should be clear that taken literally — deploy N models and average outputs — ensembling is the weakest compression technique and strictly increases cost.
checks.explanation: Ensembling is the weakest compression technique and the strongest accuracy technique; its place in a compression pipeline is as a teacher, or as a soup.
